title: ROUNDUP and ROUNDDOWN: one direction only

screens.prompt: In B6, work out the crates needed: twelve units to a crate, and a part crate still ships.

hints.syntax: ROUNDUP takes the number and how many decimals to keep: =ROUNDUP(B5/12,0).
hints.func-roundup: ROUNDUP is the one that moves away from zero, and a part crate still has to be ordered.
hints.whole-crates: Crates are whole things, so the second argument is 0 decimals.
hints.require-ref: Take the total from B5 instead of typing 476, so the crate count follows the unit counts.
hints.value: 476 units is a bit under 40 crates of twelve. A part crate still ships, so the answer is the next whole crate up.
hints.error: A part crate rounded with ROUNDDOWN leaves 476 units short of a crate and the order with no crates at all once the shortfall passes a full crate.

ROUND happens to answer 40 here, but it would drop to 39 the moment the total fell below 474
two decimals keeps the part crate as 39.67, which is not a number of crates to order

screens.prompt: Now in B6, count only the crates that are completely full.

hints.syntax: =ROUNDDOWN(B5/12,0) takes the number and the decimals to keep.
hints.func-rounddown: A full crate is the part crate thrown away, so this is the direction that moves toward zero.
hints.whole-crates: Crates are counted in whole numbers, so the second argument is 0.
hints.require-ref: Divide the total in B5 rather than the 476 typed in, so the answer follows the sheet.
hints.value: 476 units is 39 full crates with 8 units left over, so the count of completely full crates is 39.
hints.error: Dividing the answer by zero returns #DIV/0!; ROUNDDOWN itself only fails when the digits argument is not a number.

ROUNDUP counts the part crate and answers 40, which claims a crate that is not full
ROUND answers 40 here, and rounding to the nearest never promises to stay low
39.67 is a decimal, and a full crate is counted in whole numbers
the total typed into the formula, so the count stops following the unit column
476 is already a whole number, so nothing is divided into crates
a crate count divided by zero returns #DIV/0!

docs.explain: The three items add up to 476 units and a crate holds twelve. 476 divided by 12 is 39.67, which is not a number of crates you can order, so one of the two one-way functions has to decide. ROUNDUP moves away from zero and gives 40: thirty-nine full crates and a part crate that still has to ship. ROUNDDOWN moves toward zero and gives 39: the full crates only, with 8 units left on the floor. ROUND would give 40 today, which is why it is the wrong tool here. It agrees by luck and would answer 39 the moment the total dropped below 474, so the count would change direction without anyone noticing.

errors.text: The digits argument was text or a range, so the number could not be rounded.
The crate count was divided by zero, usually because the units-per-crate cell it pointed at had not been filled in yet.

docs.atWork: Ordering packing crates, where a part crate still costs the same as a full one and a short order means units sitting on the floor.
docs.outcome: Round a decimal up or down on purpose instead of letting the nearest value decide.
docs.dataset: Three items and a crate size

seo.title: ROUNDUP and ROUNDDOWN in Excel
seo.description: 476 units at twelve to a crate is 39.67. ROUNDUP orders 40 crates because the part crate ships, ROUNDDOWN counts 39 full ones, and ROUND agrees by luck.
